Longformer uses a sliding window pattern in which each token attends only to its neighbors within a window of 512 tokens [2][1]. This restricts the number of computed scores to grow linearly rather than quadratically with sequence length [2].

BigBird combines a sliding window with a set of global tokens and randomly chosen connections between positions [1]. The sliding window limits the attention to nearby tokens, while the global tokens and random connections allow information to propagate beyond the window [1]. This combination keeps the expressive power of full attention while using only linear memory and reducing the attention cost [1].

Longformer and BigBird reduce the cost of attention by using sparse attention patterns. In Longformer, each token attends only to its neighbors within a sliding window of 512 tokens [2]. This restricts the number of computed scores to grow linearly rather than quadratically with the sequence length. 

BigBird combines a sliding window, a set of global tokens, and randomly chosen connections between positions [1]. The global tokens allow attending to the whole sequence, while the randomly chosen connections between positions enable the model to keep the expressive power of full attention while using only linear memory. The combination of these ingredients allows BigBird to reduce the attention cost as well [1].

So in summary, both Longformer and BigBird achieve a reduction in attention cost by restricting the number of computed scores to grow linearly with sequence length, rather than quadratically, through the use of sliding window patterns and sparse connections [2][1].

(2) Sparse attention replaces the full attention matrix with a sparse subset of attention connections [1]. This reduces the number of computations and memory required by only attending to a subset of tokens. 

Linear attention approximates the attention matrix using a kernel feature map, allowing the attention computation to be performed in linear time with respect to sequence length n [5]. State space models represent the attention mechanism as a dynamical system, where the parameters of the network are coupled with a set of state parameters. This allows the attention to be computed in a more efficient manner by reusing computations across time steps [2].

Sparse attention, linear attention, and state space models each have different trade-offs in terms of computational complexity, scalability, and expressiveness:

Sparse attention methods, such as Block-Sparse and Random Patterns [1][2], restrict each token to attend to only a small subset of positions. This results in linear memory usage and linear growth of computed scores with sequence length, making it hardware-friendly and scalable to long inputs [1]. However, sparse attention may lose some accuracy on tasks that require precise recall of distant dependencies [1].

Linear attention, like in Longformer using a sliding window pattern [4][5], restricts each token to attend to its neighbors within a fixed window size. This also leads to linear memory and linear growth in computation, enabling efficient processing of long sequences [4]. However, the receptive field is limited to the window size and does not grow with depth, potentially missing long-range dependencies [4].

State space models process the sequence with a recurrence that maintains a fixed-size hidden state [3]. The cost scales linearly with sequence length, and the model can decide what to remember or forget at each step through selective state spaces [3]. This approach achieves higher inference throughput compared to a comparable Transformer [3]. However, the fixed-size hidden state may not capture very long-range dependencies as effectively as sparse or linear attention methods [3].

In summary, sparse attention offers linear memory and scalability but may sacrifice some accuracy for distant dependencies [1]. Linear attention provides linear complexity and receptive field growth but limited long-range dependency capture [4]. State space models achieve high throughput and linear scaling but may struggle with very long-range dependencies due to the fixed-size hidden state [3]. The choice among these methods depends on the specific requirements of the task, such as the need for precise recall, long-range dependency handling, or computational efficiency [1][4][3].

This makes sparse attention hardware-friendly and memory-efficient, as it uses only linear memory [5]. However, the survey notes that no single mechanism dominates, and linear attention can lose accuracy on tasks that require precise recall [1].

Linear attention replaces the softmax with a kernel feature map, allowing the product of queries and keys to be computed in time linear in n. This makes linear attention attractive for very long inputs, as it scales linearly with sequence length [7]. However, the survey also states that linear attention can lose accuracy on tasks that need precise recall [1].

State space models process a sequence with a recurrence that carries a fixed-size hidden state, so their cost scales linearly with length [3]. The survey reports that state space models achieve roughly five times higher inference throughput than a comparable Transformer [3]. However, the survey notes that state space models currently offer the best throughput at long context lengths, but no single mechanism dominates [1].

In summary, sparse attention is hardware-friendly and memory-efficient but may lose accuracy on tasks requiring precise recall [5][1]. Linear attention is attractive for very long inputs but can lose accuracy on tasks needing precise recall [7][1]. State space models scale linearly with length and achieve high throughput but are currently the best option for long context lengths [3][1]. The survey concludes that no single mechanism dominates, and the trade-offs depend on the specific requirements of the task [1].

(2) The Transformer architecture computes attention using the Scaled Dot-Product Attention mechanism [3][4]. In this attention function, the query, key, and value vectors are first linearly projected to different dimensions (dk, dk, dv) [4]. The query is then multiplied by the transpose of the key and divided by √dk to obtain the attention scores [3][4]. These scores are passed through a softmax function to obtain the attention weights [3][4]. Finally, the values are multiplied by these attention weights and summed to produce the output of the attention layer [3][4]. In BERT, this attention mechanism is applied in a multi-head configuration, where multiple parallel attention heads are used to attend to different representation subspaces simultaneously [2][4].

The attention function is defined as:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √dk)V

SpectralRepNet uses the structural re-parameterization technique introduced by RepVGG to enable real-time image dehazing on edge surveillance devices [1][4]. Specifically, SpectralRepNet applies the same multi-branch architecture and structural re-parameterization methodology as RepVGG, which allows the model to be trained with an ensemble of shallower models and then transformed into a single 3x3 convolution layer for inference [4]. This enables SpectralRepNet to achieve real-time performance on edge devices while maintaining high dehazing quality [1].

SpectralRepNet uses the structural re-parameterization technique introduced by RepVGG by incorporating a RepVGGBlock into its architecture. The RepVGGBlock is a multi-branch training-time architecture that can be transformed into a single 3×3 convolution during inference, as described in [7]. This allows SpectralRepNet to achieve real-time performance on edge hardware like the NVIDIA Jetson Nano while keeping the model small with only 0.38M parameters [8]. The key aspects of RepVGG's structural re-parameterization that SpectralRepNet leverages include using identity and 1×1 branches, performing training-time multi-branching to compensate for limited width, and enabling inference-time simplification to a single convolution [7].

(1) The RepVGG paper uses three branches during training: a 3×3 convolution branch, a 1×1 convolution branch, and an identity branch [1][2]. The training-time architecture is constructed with these multi-branch topology inspired by ResNet, but the branches can be removed for inference [1].

(2) At inference time, the three branches are fused into a single 3×3 convolution kernel using structural re-parameterization [1][4]. The fused kernel is obtained by adding the 3×3 convolution kernel, the 1×1 convolution kernel (with its values positioned in the center of the 3×3 kernel), and the identity kernel (which is a 3×3 kernel with a value of 1 in the central element and zeros elsewhere) [4]. This transformation allows the inference-time model to have a plain architecture composed of only 3×3 convolutions and ReLU layers, making it faster on generic computing devices like GPUs [1][4]. The equivalence of this transformation requires the same stride and appropriate padding configuration [4].

(1) The RepVGG paper uses three branches during training: a 3 × 3 convolution branch, a 1 × 1 convolution branch, and an identity branch [1][2]. The training process involves computing the output as y = W3x3 ∗x + W1x1 ∗x + x, where W3x3 is the kernel of the 3 × 3 convolution branch, W1x1 is the kernel of the 1 × 1 convolution branch, and x is the input [2]. The gradients from these three branches are used to force the network to learn more features during training [1].

(2) At inference time, the RepVGG paper uses a single 3 × 3 convolution kernel to replace the three branches. This is achieved through a structural re-parameterization technique, which fuses the three branches into one 3 × 3 kernel. The fusion formula is Wdeploy = W3x3 + pad(W1x1) + Ikernel, where W3x3 is the kernel of the 3 × 3 convolution branch, W1x1 is the kernel of the 1 × 1 convolution branch, Ikernel is a 3 × 3 kernel with a value of 1 in the central element of each channel and zeros elsewhere, and pad(W1x1) shifts the 1 × 1 kernel by one pixel [2]. This transformation allows the model to run faster on GPUs and specialized inference chips, as it only requires a stack of 3 × 3 conv layers with ReLU activations [8].
